preamble: The shift of the voiceless dental fricative [θ] to the labiodental [f] is a context-free change driven by the acoustic similarity of the two weak, non-sibilant fricatives. It is best known as th-fronting in English dialects (Cockney, Estuary, AAVE, Bristol, Glasgow), but it has occurred independently in early Italic, where the *θ from PIE *dʰ became word-initial f (Latin fūmus, faciō). The reverse change f > θ is rare.

examples.note: Classic London th-fronting, recorded for 'low English' of London as early as 1787.
The *θ that PIE *dʰ gave word-initially became f; compare Greek θῡμός, which keeps the dental.

sources: Blevins, J. (2019). Deconstructing markedness in sound change typology: Notes on θ > f and f > θ. In Perspectives on Language Structure and Language Change (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 345), 107–122. John Benjamins. https://doi.org/10.1075/cilt.345.04ble
